sysd-reliab-042.title: Docker run workflow: from docker run to a running container
sysd-reliab-042.text: What actually happens when you type docker run? Docker has three components: a client that talks to the daemon, a host whose daemon listens for API requests, and a registry that stores images. The daemon manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks and volumes. When docker run executes, Docker pulls the image from the registry, creates a new container and allocates a read-write filesystem to it. It then creates a network interface that connects the container to the default network, and starts the container.

sysd-reliab-047.title: Docker Compose: a multi-container application from one command
sysd-reliab-047.text: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications, and it creates and starts all the containers with a single command. It uses YAML files to configure the application's services. The docker-compose.yml file defines those services and their configuration options, such as the path of the Dockerfile used to build one. The docker compose command-line utility then runs commands on several containers at once, for example building images, scaling containers or restarting stopped ones.

sysd-reliab-048.title: Docker Swarm: several Docker engines acting as one
sysd-reliab-048.text: Docker Swarm provides native clustering for Docker containers, turning a group of Docker engines into a single virtual Docker engine. A Docker service lets containers be scaled across multiple Docker daemons. The resulting set of cooperating daemons, communicating through the Docker API, is a swarm, integrated into Docker Engine since Docker 1.12. Swarm is managed with the Raft consensus algorithm (see {{ref:sysd-scale-021}}), so a majority of Swarm nodes must agree before an update is performed. The docker stack tool manages Swarm services with a configuration file very like docker-compose.yml, and can manage a Swarm cluster across multiple machines.

sysd-reliab-065.title: Virtual machine: a whole computer made of software
sysd-reliab-065.text: Most deployments use only a small part of a server's physical resources, which is the opening that virtual machines fill. A virtual machine is the virtualization or emulation of a computer system that provides the functionality of a physical computer. It runs as a virtual computer with its own CPU, memory, network interface and storage, created on a physical hardware system. The physical hardware is the host and the emulated machine is the guest; one host can emulate several guests, each running a different operating system. Server consolidation is a top reason for using them: many virtual servers can be placed on each physical server to improve utilization. Because a VM is isolated, what runs inside cannot interfere with the host, which suits testing new applications, setting up production environments and isolating applications for security. System virtual machines substitute for a real machine and can execute entire operating systems. A process virtual machine instead runs a single program in a platform-independent environment, and the Java virtual machine is a well-known example.

sysd-reliab-044.title: Hypervisor: the software that creates and runs virtual machines
sysd-reliab-044.text: One machine can run several operating systems at once, and if one crashes the others keep working. A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, is the software, firmware or hardware that makes this possible by creating and running virtual machines. The machine it runs on is the host and each virtual machine is a guest. The hypervisor presents guest operating systems with a virtual platform and treats CPU, memory and storage as a pool that can be reallocated between guests. Unlike an emulator, the guest executes most instructions on native hardware. Type-1, or bare-metal, hypervisors run directly on the host's hardware, as Hyper-V, Xen and VMware ESXi do. Type-2 hypervisors run on a conventional operating system like any other program, as VirtualBox and VMware Workstation do. Modern hypervisors use hardware-assisted virtualization, and Intel and AMD released their first x86 processors with it in 2005.

sysd-reliab-043.title: Virtualization versus containerization: a guest OS or a shared kernel
sysd-reliab-043.text: A virtual machine brings its own operating system along. A container borrows the host's. In traditional virtualization a hypervisor virtualizes the physical hardware. Each virtual machine then holds a guest operating system, a virtual copy of the hardware it needs, and the application with its libraries and dependencies. Containers virtualize the operating system instead of the hardware, so each contains only the application and its dependencies. That is why containers are much more lightweight: they share the OS kernel and use a fraction of the memory VMs require. They use just the computing resources they need, whereas VMs raise hardware utilization by placing many virtual servers on one physical server.

sysd-reliab-066.title: Virtual machine snapshots and migration: an undo button for a whole machine
sysd-reliab-066.text: Restoring a virtual machine snapshot undoes every change made since. A snapshot is the state of a virtual machine at an exact point in time, which makes it a useful backup technique before a risky operation. Each snapshot creates a new file used as an overlay for its predecessors. New data goes to the topmost overlay, and reads scan the hierarchy for the most recent version. A snapshot can also move to another host machine with its own hypervisor. Stopping the VM, snapshotting, moving and resuming it there is known as migration. Failover ({{ref:sysd-scale-058}}) is similar and lets the VM keep operating if its host fails.

sysd-reliab-149.title: Physical, virtual and container deployment: three eras of running applications
sysd-reliab-149.text: On physical servers, an application's resources could not be bounded, so one application could take most of them and leave others underperforming. One application per server did not scale either, because resources were underused and servers were costly. Virtualization runs several virtual machines on one server's CPU, isolating applications and improving utilization, but each VM is a full machine with its own operating system. Containers relax the isolation to share the operating system, so they are lightweight. Each has its own filesystem, share of CPU, memory and process space, and is portable across clouds and OS distributions. They also give faster image creation than VM images.

sysd-reliab-143.title: Continuous delivery: always ready to release
sysd-reliab-143.text: Continuous delivery bets that releasing often is safer than releasing rarely. It is a software engineering approach in which teams produce software in short cycles, ensuring that it can be reliably released at any time. Every commit is built and packaged by a build server and tested by several techniques before it can be marked releasable. The deployment pipeline is the set of validations a change must pass on its way to release. Its purpose is visibility, feedback and continually deploying any version to any environment through full automation. The approach brings the pain forward: tough tasks are tackled early, which fosters automation and swift issue detection. Frequent releases carry fewer changes each, so problems are easier to find and fix and their impact lasts a shorter time. Code not yet ready for users can be committed early (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-141}}), because long-lived branches become impractical. Obstacles include a lack of test automation, differences between development, test and production environments, tests that need a human oracle, and regulated domains needing customer-side or on-site testing.

sysd-reliab-144.title: CI/CD pipeline: from a merged change to a deployed one
sysd-reliab-144.text: CI/CD combines continuous integration with continuous delivery or, less often, continuous deployment. A CI/CD pipeline is three processes in order. First comes frequent merging of small changes into a main branch. Then software is produced in short cycles so it can be released at any time. Last comes automatic rollout of new functionality. The services compile the incremental code changes, then link and package them into deliverables. Automated tests verify the functionality and automated deployment services deliver it to end users. The aim is early defect discovery, higher productivity and faster release cycles. Traditional methods instead integrated a collection of updates into one large batch before deploying. Small teams can be more productive with one repository and one pipeline, whereas larger organizations may have separate ones for each team or even each service. Least privilege is hard to apply to pipeline permissions because the architecture is dynamic. Administrators may allow more permissive permissions while adding compensating security controls to limit the blast radius.

sysd-reliab-162.title: Release engineering: making releases repeatable rather than unique
sysd-reliab-162.text: Reliable services need reliable release processes, and that means no unique snowflakes. Release engineering is the discipline of building and delivering software, defining every step from source storage and build rules to testing, packaging and deployment. Binaries and configurations are built reproducibly and automatically, so releases are repeatable and changes to the release process are intentional. In the self-service model, product teams run their own release processes and decide how often to release, with releases automated until problems need an engineer. High velocity rests on the view that frequent releases mean fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier. Some teams build hourly and pick the build to deploy from test results. Several layers of access control gate who can approve source changes, create a release, approve cherry picks, deploy a release or change build configuration. Almost all changes need code review. Teams should budget for release engineering at the start, since good practice put in early is cheaper than retrofitting it.

sysd-reliab-147.title: Infrastructure as code: servers described in files, not set up by hand
sysd-reliab-147.text: Instead of building a server's configuration by hand, you apply a pre-set one. That is infrastructure as code: managing and provisioning data center resources through machine-readable definition files rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. The infrastructure covers bare-metal servers, virtual machines and their configuration. Definitions live in version control, so infrastructure is treated like software, reviewed and deployed automatically, which reduces manual errors and lets teams reproduce environments reliably. The declarative approach defines the desired state and the system works out what to do. The imperative approach lists the commands to run in order. IaC more often uses declarative definitions. In the push method the controlling system sends instructions directly to the server, and in the pull method the server retrieves its own. Tools include CFEngine, Puppet, Chef, SaltStack, Ansible and Terraform. The templates themselves need security review: a 2020 cloud threat report identified around 200,000 potential vulnerabilities in infrastructure-as-code templates.

sysd-reliab-041.title: Twelve-factor app: principles for an application that scales and behaves
sysd-reliab-041.text: Twelve principles describe an application that is reliable, scalable and manageable. Keep all code in one place under version control such as Git, and list every dependency so the app is easy to install. Keep settings such as database credentials separate from code, so they can change without rewriting it. Treat other services, such as databases or payment processors, as separate components the app connects to. Separate the stages of preparing the app, releasing it and running it in production. Design processes so that no part relies on a specific computer or its memory. Expose the app through a network port, without storing critical information on a single machine. Handle more work by adding more copies of the same process, and make each process start quickly and shut down gracefully. Keep development very similar to production to avoid surprises, record what the app does in logs, and run special administrative tasks separately from the app.

sysd-reliab-059.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets: configuration that changes without a rebuild
sysd-reliab-059.text: Kubernetes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default. They are designed for confidential data such as certificates, registry credentials, passwords and ssh keys, so they need extra setup to be fully secured. With ConfigMaps they form two closely related mechanisms for storing configuration, so that changes need no rebuild of the application. A pod receives the data as environment variables or as files in a mounted volume, and volume mounts reload automatically without a container restart. A ConfigMap or Secret goes to a node only if a pod there requires it, is held only in memory, and is deleted with that pod.

sysd-reliab-165.title: Hermetic builds: the same revision, the same result, on any machine
sysd-reliab-165.text: Build the same product at the same source revision on different machines, and the results should be identical. A hermetic build is insensitive to the software installed on the build machine. It depends on known versions of build tools such as compilers and of dependencies such as libraries, and relies on no services external to the build environment. Build tools are themselves versioned by source revision. A project built last month therefore does not use this month's compiler when a cherry pick forces a rebuild, since that compiler may have incompatible features. Every binary can display its build date, revision number and build identifier.

sysd-reliab-164.title: Release branching and cherry-picking: fixing a release without moving it
sysd-reliab-164.text: Most major projects do not release from the mainline. All code is checked into it, but releases come from a branch cut at a specific revision, and changes are never merged from the branch back. Bug fixes go to the mainline first and are then cherry picked into the release branch. That avoids picking up unrelated changes and means the exact contents of each release are known. To fix a bug in an older release, rebuild at the same revision as the original build and include the specific later changes. This tactic is called cherry picking. Each cherry pick request is approved or rejected individually.

sysd-reliab-163.title: Release pipeline: how a revision becomes a signed, canaried package
sysd-reliab-163.text:
How does a source revision become something deployable? A release pipeline turns a tested revision into a deployable package by branching, building, testing, packaging and canarying, and it logs each step. It starts with a continuous test system that runs unit tests on the mainline at every submitted change. Releases are cut at the revision of the last continuous test build that passed all tests, so release-time builds are less likely to fail.

The pipeline creates a release branch from the requested integration revision, then compiles the binaries and runs unit tests, often in parallel, in environments dedicated to those tasks. Unit tests are re-run on the release branch with an audit trail, because cherry picks can leave a branch with code that exists nowhere on the mainline.

Packages are named, versioned with a unique hash and signed. Labels such as dev, canary and production mark a package's place in the release, and reapplying a label moves it to the newest package. Build artifacts then go to system testing and canary deployments; a typical canary starts a few jobs in production after system tests finish. Each step's result is logged, and a report of all changes since the last release is created.

sysd-reliab-155.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adding Pods when load rises
sysd-reliab-155.text: When load rises, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds Pods, and when it falls, it takes them away. It automatically updates a workload resource such as a Deployment or StatefulSet to scale capacity to match demand, which is the idea of {{ref:sysd-q-067}} applied to Pods. Horizontal scaling responds to increased load by deploying more Pods, unlike vertical scaling, which would give the running Pods more memory or CPU. The autoscaler is an API resource plus a controller in the control plane, running a control loop intermittently, by default every 15 seconds. Each period it reads metrics, and a utilization target is a percentage of the Pod's resource request. The core calculation is desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue): a current value of 200m against a desired 100m doubles the replicas, and 50m halves them. The control plane skips scaling when the ratio is close enough to 1.0, within a tolerance that defaults to 0.1. With several metrics, each is evaluated and the largest desired replica count is used, up to the configured maximum.

sysd-reliab-156.title: Autoscaler flapping controls: stopping the replica count from swinging
sysd-reliab-156.text: Replica counts can fluctuate frequently as the evaluated metrics change, which is called thrashing or flapping. On scale-down the autoscaler uses the highest desired count from a stabilization window, a rolling maximum. That way it does not remove Pods only to recreate them moments later. The default window is 300 seconds. Scaling policies cap the rate of change as a number of Pods or a percentage per period. By default scale-up adds at most 4 Pods or 100% of the running replicas every 15 seconds. A tolerance of 10% makes the autoscaler ignore changes inside the threshold.

sysd-reliab-157.title: Scaling to zero: no replicas while a workload is idle
sysd-reliab-157.text: Some workloads sit idle for long periods and are expensive to keep running, such as consumers of an occasionally used queue or jobs needing dedicated hardware like GPUs. Scaling to zero lets an autoscaler reduce such a workload to no replicas and bring it back when a metric shows demand. It works with custom (object) or external metrics, where minReplicas can be set to 0. It is not available for resource metrics such as CPU or memory, which can only be measured on running Pods. While a workload is held at zero, the autoscaler sets a ScaledToZero condition, which tells it apart from one deactivated manually.

sysd-reliab-160.title: Pod requests and limits: what a container asks for and may use
sysd-reliab-160.text: A container can tell Kubernetes how much CPU and memory it needs and how much it may use, and those declarations drive scheduling and enforcement. The kube-scheduler uses the resource requests of a Pod's containers to decide which node to place the Pod on. The kubelet enforces limits so a running container cannot use more than its limit. CPU limits work by throttling, where the kernel restricts CPU access, and memory limits by out-of-memory kills. Autoscaling measures utilization as current usage divided by the Pod's requested resources, so requests must be set. Without one, CPU utilization is undefined and the autoscaler takes no action. A Pod's CPU and memory can also change after creation. In-place resize updates the desired state through the /resize subresource, and the kubelet applies it to running containers. Only CPU and memory can be resized, and resizePolicy says whether a restart is needed. Resizing by replacement works on any Kubernetes version and can change any Pod specification, but it replaces Pods, so the workload must tolerate planned disruptions.

sysd-reliab-150.title: Rolling update: replacing a version one instance at a time
sysd-reliab-150.text: A rolling update swaps old instances for new ones one by one, so the application stays available throughout. A Deployment's strategy type is RollingUpdate, the default, or Recreate. A rolling update gradually scales down the old ReplicaSets and scales up the new one, and it suits periodic releases. Recreate kills all existing Pods before creating new ones, which suits non-critical applications or early development. Two settings set the pace. The first, maxUnavailable, caps the Pods that may be unavailable during the update. The second, maxSurge, caps the Pods created above the desired number. Each is a number or a percentage, and each defaults to 25%: a percentage is rounded down for maxUnavailable and up for maxSurge. With maxUnavailable at 30%, at least 70% of desired Pods stay available, and with maxSurge at 30% the total never exceeds 130% of desired. They cannot both be 0, so at least one must allow change. The minReadySeconds setting is how long a new Pod must be ready without a crash before it counts as available, and it defaults to 0.

sysd-reliab-056.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets: the right number of Pods, and undo
sysd-reliab-056.text: A bad rollout can be undone because Kubernetes keeps the old version around. A ReplicaSet keeps a stable set of replica pods running at any given time, and uses a selector to identify the pods associated with it. A Deployment is the higher-level mechanism that manages ReplicaSets, usually for a workload that keeps no state. You declare the desired state, and the Deployment controller changes the actual state to match it at a controlled rate. The ReplicaSet controller manages the scale, while the Deployment controller manages what happens to the ReplicaSet, such as whether an update is rolled out or rolled back. Updating the Pod template (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-158}}) creates a new ReplicaSet that is scaled up as the old one is scaled down. A Deployment's revision history is kept in its old ReplicaSets, 10 by default; once an old one is deleted, that revision can no longer be rolled back to. A Deployment is progressing, complete or failed to progress, and progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) sets how long to wait before reporting failure.

sysd-reliab-057.title: StatefulSets: giving each instance an identity and an order
sysd-reliab-057.text: Scaling a stateless application only means adding more pods. Stateful workloads are harder, because state must be preserved when a pod restarts and may need to be redistributed when scaling. A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes controller that enforces uniqueness and ordering among the instances of a pod so that such applications can run. Both properties matter. Databases are stateful, and in high-availability mode many have a primary and secondary instances, so the ordering of instances matters. Applications such as Apache Kafka distribute data among their brokers, so one broker is not the same as another and instance uniqueness matters.
